sections.category: The EU AI Act's transparency article starts applying and the Commission opens enforcement alongside national authorities

bullets.body: Article 50 of the EU AI Act starts applying today, and the European Commission marked the date by confirming that its AI Office and national authorities are now enforcing it. Four situations are covered: an AI system that interacts directly with a person has to say it is an AI, synthetic image, audio, video and text has to carry machine-readable marks so it can be detected, deployers of emotion-recognition and biometric-categorisation systems have to tell the people exposed to them, and deepfakes and AI-generated text published on matters of public interest have to be labelled. Enforcement sits with national market surveillance authorities, the AI Office and the European Data Protection Supervisor, with fines reaching €15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover for companies and €750,000 for EU institutions, bodies and agencies, and proportionality for small and medium enterprises written into the framework. The scaffolding went up before the date rather than on it: the Commission adopted its Article 50 guidelines on Monday, July 20, and the accompanying Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content — the voluntary route to demonstrating compliance, which carries a free EU icon set for labelling — has now passed 180 signatories, with a first list published. The AI Act itself entered into force on August 1, 2024.

sections.category: California's AI Transparency Act becomes operative on the same date the EU's does, and the collision is deliberate

bullets.body: California's AI Transparency Act became operative today as well, and the alignment was engineered: SB 942 as passed said the chapter would become operative on January 1, 2026, and AB 853 rewrote that clause to read August 2, 2026 — the same day Article 50 starts applying in the EU. The law binds any provider of a generative AI system with more than one million monthly visitors or users that is publicly accessible in California. Those providers must embed a latent disclosure in the images, video and audio their system produces — the provider's name, the system's name and version, the time and date the content was created or altered, and a unique identifier — offer users an optional visible label, and publish a free detection tool that supports an application programming interface a user can invoke without visiting the provider's website, which accepts a URL, returns whatever provenance data it finds, and does not retain submitted content longer than it needs to. A provider that licenses its system out has to require the same latent-disclosure capability by contract and revoke the licence within 96 hours of discovering the licensee stripped it. The penalty is $5,000 per violation with each day of non-compliance counted separately, and the California Attorney General, a city attorney or a county counsel can each bring the action, with fees and costs to a prevailing plaintiff. Two further tranches are already dated: generative AI hosting platforms and large online platforms on January 1, 2027, and capture device manufacturers on January 1, 2028.

sections.category: Unsloth ships 2026.8.1 to PyPI with DeepSeek-V4 0731 support and moves its installer pins onto it the same day

bullets.body: Unsloth published version 2026.8.1 to PyPI today, its first new version since 2026.7.6 on Wednesday, July 29. It stays Apache-2.0 and still supports Python 3.9 up to but not including 3.15. The changelog frames the release as a continuation of the 2026.7.6 Kimi K3 release and lists three things: support for DeepSeek-V4 0731, a batch of Windows fixes, and general bug fixes across models and systems. A merge later the same day raised the pin in both `install.sh` and `install.ps1` to `unsloth>=2026.8.1` and `unsloth-zoo>=2026.8.1` across all five install paths, so a fresh install now resolves to the new packages rather than the July ones. Two of the day's other merges were escaping fixes on the path where caller-supplied strings meet the template engine. One escapes template text spliced into Jinja string literals, where an apostrophe in something like "user's question" would close the literal early and raise a template syntax error, and an unescaped backslash was silently decoded — `\boxed{}` became a backspace followed by `oxed{}`, and a Windows path like `C:\Users\me` broke outright; the second promotes that escape helper to module level, extends it to double quotes, and applies it to the system message substituted into the predefined chat templates, taking successful renderings from 76 of 180 to 180 of 180 across fifteen predefined templates and twelve test messages.

sections.category: Karpathy says the field is starting to leave the pelican prompt behind, after a two-hour, million-token render of Tolkien

bullets.body: The most-discussed item of the day was a test rather than a release. Andrej Karpathy handed Claude Opus 5 the opening paragraph of The Lord of the Rings, a budget of one million tokens costing roughly $10, and a request for a three.js rendering. The model worked for about two hours and produced roughly 5,500 lines of code that procedurally rendered the passage, placing and animating polygon assets in three-dimensional coordinates; Karpathy called the result janky but fun, and said the field is starting to leave the territory where you would test a model by asking it for an SVG of a pelican on a bicycle. The shape of the test is the point, not the artefact: one prompt, a large budget, a long unattended run, and a judgement on whether what comes back holds together is a different measurement from scoring a single completion, and it is a measurement that only recently became cheap enough to run casually.

citations.label: Developers Digest - Beyond the pelican test, Opus 5 renders the Lord of the Rings with a 1M-token budget
Benzinga - Andrej Karpathy says AI has moved beyond simple prompts after Claude Opus builds a 3D Lord of the Rings world

sections.category: A 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 returns more tokens per dollar on eight MI355X than on eight B300 and loses on raw speed, with speculative decoding described on only one side of the comparison

bullets.body: A benchmark posted Friday, July 31 and picked up over the weekend put Kimi K3, at 2.8 trillion parameters, on three configurations and came back with a split verdict for AMD. On eight AMD MI355X running SGLang with ROCm fixes and speculative decoding from RadixArk's Kimi-K3-DSpark draft model, a 1,024-token input and 400-token output workload decoded at 118 tokens per second single-stream and peaked at 952 tokens per second aggregate, or 119 per GPU. Eight NVIDIA B300 beat that outright at 172 single-stream, 1,568 aggregate and 196 per GPU, and a two-node, sixteen-GPU B200 configuration came last at 90 single-stream and 498 aggregate, 31 per GPU. The ordering inverts on cost: at $2.50 per GPU-hour the MI355X box returns about 48 tokens per second per dollar-hour against about 33 for the B300 at $6.00 per GPU-hour and about 7 for the two-node B200 at $4.25 per GPU-hour. The reason the author gives is capacity rather than compute — enough HBM on the AMD box to hold a model this size without spanning nodes, which is what drags the two-node B200 configuration down to 31 tokens per second per GPU. One asymmetry sits under the comparison: the speculative decoding credited with about 2.2 times the single-stream rate on the MI355X box has no counterpart described for either NVIDIA configuration, both of which the benchmark lists as running CUDA, so the cost ordering is not a hardware-only result.

citations.label: Wafer - Running Kimi K3 on MI355X at better performance per dollar than B300

sections.category: Bay Area / SV AI meet-up events

bullets.body:
The Las Vegas security stretch is now underway. Black Hat USA 2026 opened yesterday at Mandalay Bay and runs to Thursday, August 6: trainings from Saturday, August 1 through Tuesday, August 4, six summits on Tuesday, August 4 including the one-day AI Summit, then briefings on Wednesday, August 5 and Thursday, August 6. DEF CON 34 picks up on Thursday, August 6 and runs to Sunday, August 9 at the LVCC West Hall, $520 cash at the door, with a badge built on bunnie Huang's open-source Baochip that keeps working afterwards as a security token, password manager and hardware security module. The AI Village takes Room W603 on Level 1 of the LVCC from August 6 with competitions, Creator Stage talks, poster presentations, fireside chats and demos, and runs HalCTF — the Hostile Autonomous Layer capture-the-flag — where teams of up to five deploy an agent that has to exploit sandboxed targets and capture flags on its own, with the models hosted for entrants so the entry cost is code rather than GPUs. Ai4 is at The Venetian in Las Vegas from Tuesday, August 4 to Thursday, August 6, and FMS: The Future of Memory and Storage marks its twentieth year at the Santa Clara Convention Center and the Hyatt Regency across the same three days.

Hot Chips 2026's early-registration rate is gone — that deadline was 11:59 PM PDT on Friday, July 31 — so anyone booking now pays standard, and late registration stays open through the conference itself, though in-person capacity can sell out. Refunds can be requested until 11:59 PM PDT on Wednesday, August 19, less a $25 processing fee. The symposium runs Sunday, August 23 to Tuesday, August 25 at Memorial Auditorium at Stanford in Palo Alto and is hybrid, with the virtual pass carrying videos, presentation PDFs and Slack channels for both the tutorial and the conference days. Sunday, August 23 is the tutorial day, a memory tutorial in the morning and a RISC-V tutorial in the afternoon. The conference days are Monday, August 24 and Tuesday, August 25: two CPU sessions spanning IBM's Z and LinuxONE processor, Intel's Core Series 3 Wildcat Lake and Diamond Rapids Xeon, NVIDIA's Vera CPU, Fujitsu's MONAKA and an Arm server part for AI workloads; a Waymo keynote on autonomous driving plus an automotive session with BOS Semiconductors' Eagle-N and Waymo's sensor-fusion processor; a GPU session with NVIDIA's Rubin, AMD's Instinct MI400 Series and Intel's Crescent Island. Tuesday adds an FPGA session in which AMD presents a secure computing SoC alongside Versal RF — worth a note for anyone tracking the security-silicon intersection — a memory session with Samsung's LPDDR5X processing-in-memory part and XCENA's MX1 CXL device, a networking session with Broadcom's Thor Ultra, NVIDIA's BlueField-4 and Spectrum-X and Mojo Vision's optical I/O, and two accelerator sessions covering Meta's MTIA, an NVIDIA LPU accelerator, Cerebras' Wafer Scale Engine, Microsoft's MAIA 200, SambaNova's SN50 RDU, Google's TPU family and OpenAI on its chip development.

Closest to home on the security track, SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit is at the Ritz-Carlton in Half Moon Bay on Tuesday, August 11 and Wednesday, August 12. The full pass is $1,895 and steps to $2,195 after Friday, August 7; it covers the co-located CISO Forum, a welcome reception on Monday, August 10, a VIP dinner over the bay on the Tuesday, breakfast, lunch and dinner across both days, s'mores by the fire pits, post-conference materials and a discounted room rate subject to availability. The SecurityWeek Golf Classic on Thursday, August 13 at Half Moon Bay is an optional, capacity-limited add-on. Two speaking deadlines now matter for anyone who would rather present than pay: Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit takes talk submissions until Monday, August 17 for its London edition on Thursday, October 8 and until Friday, August 21 for New York on Wednesday, October 21, submissions must be vendor-agnostic and practical rather than theoretical, and selected speakers attend free with travel and up to two hotel nights covered. Zenity's own events page still shows an Asia edition with no city and no date; a third-party report giving it a Tokyo date in September remains uncorroborated there, so it is not carried here. The separately-run AI Security Summit holds its San Francisco edition on Thursday, October 15 across a leadership track for the people who own AI risk and a practitioner track for the people building and breaking the systems; its San Francisco page lists a London edition and a Paris call for talks as the other 2026 stops, neither with a date, and the Nordics and Sydney editions carried here previously still do not appear on it. New on the Bay Area calendar and colliding with that same Thursday, October 15: the San Francisco AI Engineering and Infrastructure Summit, which despite the name is at the Crowne Plaza Palo Alto on El Camino Real, 8:30 AM to 3:30 PM, free to attend, closed-door and practitioner-led with the speakers already set rather than an open call.

Further out on the security calendar, SANS runs its AI Cybersecurity Summit on Monday, November 2 and Tuesday, November 3 at the Hilton Arlington Rosslyn, hybrid, at $525 for the summit alone, with a $229 room block closing October 9 and a refund cutoff of October 14; OWASP Global AppSec USA takes the Hyatt Regency San Francisco on Thursday, November 5 and Friday, November 6 with hands-on training from November 2 to 4; and the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security meets Sunday, November 15 in The Hague alongside the 33rd ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security, its paper deadline having closed on July 24, with reviews due September 7, notifications September 9 and camera-ready September 16.

On the rest of the silicon and infrastructure calendar, the AI Infra Summit returns to the Santa Clara Convention Center from Tuesday, September 15 to Thursday, September 17 with roughly 316 sessions across a main stage plus data-and-models, compute, data-movement, AI-data-centre and physical-AI tracks, two expo theatres and workshops. Then the Edge AI and Vision Innovation Forum in San Jose on Wednesday, September 16, the OCP Global Summit in San Jose from Monday, October 12 to Thursday, October 15, NVIDIA's GTC Berlin from Tuesday, October 20 to Thursday, October 22, and SC26 in Chicago from Sunday, November 15 to Friday, November 20. GTC does not return to San Jose until March 2027.

Ray Summit is at the San Francisco Marriott Marquis from Monday, August 24 to Wednesday, August 26 — a training day on the Monday, then two days of keynotes and breakouts — at $400 for the summit and $450 with training, with a five-pass bundle listed at $750 against a $2,250 list price. The training day covers multimodal data pipelines, distributed foundation-model training, production inference, physical AI and robotics, real-time search and recommendation, and post-training and serving. The first vLLM Conference is co-located, hosted by Inferact, and included in every Ray Summit pass, with more than twenty speakers across vLLM infrastructure, hardware backends, production deployment patterns and ecosystem integrations, including vLLM creator and core maintainer Woosuk Kwon, now Inferact's chief technology officer, and core maintainer Simon Mo, now its chief executive, plus contributors from NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU, Intel, Meta and PyTorch, Hugging Face and Red Hat. Ray Summit's own keynotes come from Anyscale co-founders Robert Nishihara and Ion Stoica, NVIDIA's Bryan Catanzaro, Torc's Felix Heide and Lila Sciences' Andrew Beam. The ACM AI Leadership Summit is in Atlanta from Sunday, August 30 to Wednesday, September 2.

Four San Francisco events still collide at the end of September. CoreWeave's Fully Connected is at Moscone South from Tuesday, September 29 to Thursday, October 1; its early-bird rate has lapsed, so the standard pass is $1,299 against $899 before, and three tracks cover AI infrastructure, model advances, and agent evaluation and monitoring, with a keynote roster running to CoreWeave chief executive Mike Intrator and chief technology officer Peter Salanki, NVIDIA's Ian Buck, Fei-Fei Li of Stanford and World Labs, Sarah Guo of Conviction and Liquid AI chief operating officer Jeffrey Li. The AI Conference is at Pier 48 Sheds A and B over the same window with five tracks, more than 5,500 attendees and more than 120 speakers; its September 29 workshops and Hack Day are capped at 350 and sold out, with two-day pass holders promised first notice if inventory reopens. OpenAI's DevDay is at Fort Mason on Tuesday, September 29 with applications already closed, and Newcomer's Machine Earning AI Summit is in San Francisco the same day with applications open. After that: the Runway AI Summit on Wednesday, September 30, World Summit AI in Amsterdam on Wednesday, October 7 and Thursday, October 8, the PyTorch Conference in San Jose on Tuesday, October 20 and Wednesday, October 21, AGNTCon and MCPCon North America on Thursday, October 22 and Friday, October 23 at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center under the Linux Foundation — built around the Model Context Protocol, agent infrastructure and the security and observability of production agent systems, with the call for proposals closed since June 7, so what is left is attendance — GitHub Universe at Fort Mason on Wednesday, October 28 and Thursday, October 29, the application-only AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco from Wednesday, November 11 to Friday, November 13 with speaker submissions closing October 11, Newcomer's Cerebral Valley AI Summit in San Francisco on Thursday, November 12, AWS re:Invent from Monday, November 30 to Friday, December 4, NeurIPS in December, and The AI Summit New York on Wednesday, December 9 and Thursday, December 10.

On the robotics calendar, IEEE-RAS Humanoids 2026's workshop, tutorial and competition proposal deadline is tomorrow, Monday, August 3, and it is the last open submission window — the paper deadline closed on July 27 and the supplementary-video window on July 30. Competition decisions follow on September 21, workshop and tutorial decisions on September 28, paper acceptance notifications on October 6, early-bird registration closing October 16 and camera-ready papers on October 26, with the conference itself at the Santa Clara Convention Center from Sunday, December 6 to Wednesday, December 9 — public forums on the 6th, workshops and tutorials on the 7th, and paper sessions on the 8th and 9th.

On AI Tinkerers, the London session listed for today has fired and comes off the calendar, as the New York run-and-hack session did yesterday. What is left in the near term: Columbus tomorrow, Monday, August 3, 5:30 to 8 PM EDT; Paris with Paris.rb and a Seattle AI dev-tools track on Tuesday, August 4; Singapore with Redis and an Okta-sponsored Seattle founders' dinner on trust and long-running agents on Wednesday, August 5; the Los Angeles builder meetup and live demos on Thursday, August 6, 6 to 8 PM PDT, still on the global listing after briefly dropping off it at the end of last week; a Medellín online voice-agents challenge with $1,000 in prizes and the NYC Vision Hack, 4 to 10 PM EDT, both on Friday, August 7; then the Mombasa chapter launch, edge-AI and small-model focused, and a Dubai demo day on Saturday, August 8. After that a five-city Tuesday on August 11 — Valencia, upstate New York, Chicago, Houston, and a Seattle AI-and-biology demo night with NVIDIA and the Allen Institute for AI — three more on Wednesday, August 12 in Valencia, Brussels and Raleigh, Bremen on Friday, August 14, and a newly-listed inaugural Da Nang meetup on Saturday, August 15. Nothing is dated in San Francisco, San Jose or Pleasanton. Both the Palo Alto and the San Francisco chapter pages refused the connection again today, so the Palo Alto meetup carried here for Tuesday, August 18 remains unconfirmed at its own source.
